summary:
Niger criminalises same-sex conduct and transition itself. Article 25 of the Charter of Refoundation, adopted by the military junta in March 2025, bans “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the five-year transition that followed the July 2023 coup. It was the first explicit prohibition of its kind at statutory level in the country, and it sets no penalty of its own.

The February 2026 revision of the penal code supplies the penalties. Article 390 punishes “indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts” with five to ten years' imprisonment and fines of up to 100 million CFA francs. The same article reaches public announcement of a same-sex relationship and anyone who changes or attempts to change their birth sex, which places transition-related medical and legal steps inside the criminal provision. Article 391 punishes same-sex marriage with ten to twenty years. Article 392 covers LGBTQIA+ associations. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences are excluded.

Article 392, as reported, punishes creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, with ten to twenty years in prison and fines of up to 500 million CFA francs, roughly €762,000 or US$883,000.

The drafting is broad enough that El Espectador reports asexuality as falling within the sanctionable conduct.

Enforcement has followed. By 1 July 2026 The Guardian reported at least 40 people arrested for homosexuality and 16 men imprisoned, among them high-ranking military officials; campaigners described a witch-hunt in a toxic climate. Local media reported dozens arrested across the country after the code took effect, some of them imprisoned.

State media confirmed the criminalisation: Agence Nigérienne de Presse reported on 1 June 2026 that Niger criminalises LGBTQIA+ practice under the 2026 revision.

Justice Minister Alio Daouda said “all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be” are “not in line with our social and cultural values”.

No broad legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity exists. The only provision that had touched the area, Article 4 of Law 2015-36 on Illicit Trafficking of Migrants, was repealed in 2023 by decree of President Abdourahamane Tiani, with prior convictions and their effects expunged.

Prosecutions predate the new code. In 2022 two young women in Maradi were prosecuted over lesbianism and acquitted because no legislation then criminalised it, but were imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos on social media that allegedly portrayed a lesbian act. In 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276, which carries up to three years; the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them. In Niamey in 2025 two young women reported by a third person were prosecuted for public indecency and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, and the judge was reportedly sanctioned for leniency.

In December 2022 lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by MP Nana Djibou Harouna of the southern Maradi region, weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges for want of legislation.

After the 2026 law LGBTQ people went into hiding. Historically many led socially acceptable public lives while keeping their relationships private.
tangentialFactors:
The 2023 draft penal code, circulated before the current text, proposed up to five years for same-sex conduct, twenty years for conducting, officiating or witnessing a same-sex marriage, and five years for participating in or financing homosexual organisations. The enacted 2026 provisions are heavier.

Before the 2026 revision the age of consent was unequal: 21 for same-sex acts against 13 for different-sex acts.

The revision forms part of a wider pattern of hardening legislation across the region.

President Mohamed Bazoum's 2023 proposals put “social contagion” at the centre of public discourse on the subject.

Commentary from Oxford Human Rights Hub reads the birth-sex clause in Article 390 as violating the rights of intersex people as well as LGBTQIA+ people.
localsOnly:
Organisations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working after the 2026 law. A representative warned that people no longer have access to condoms, HIV testing or PrEP, and campaigners fear an HIV/AIDS resurgence as access to PrEP collapses.

Two gay rights organisations reportedly operated in secret, partly because they were not formally registered.

Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who staged Niger's first LGBTQ public demonstration in Niamey in 2022 faced societal discrimination, including shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers. The authorities refused to recognise their refugee status.

Article 95 of Law 2022-59 on the Protection of Personal Data prohibits collecting or processing data revealing sexual orientation, punishable by three months to five years' imprisonment and fines of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs. The law was published by the Ministry of Communication and New Information Technologies in June 2025.

LGBTQIA people in Niger face stigmatisation among the broader population.
outOfScopeNotes:
The most recent official assessment in the source inventory is the U.S. State Department's 2013 Human Rights Report, which found no reports of violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity and no documented cases of discrimination, including in education, while noting that stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported; it recorded two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined. No comparable official accounting for the period since 2025 is available in the inventory.

The charter's Article 25 sets no penalty of its own, and the sources do not state how it operates alongside the penal code articles.

Whether the provision on changing or attempting to change one's birth sex reaches a visitor whose documents were amended outside the country is not addressed by the sources.

The arrest figures come from campaigners and local media rather than an official count.
